item.title: Atsuta Jingu: Shrine of the Sacred Sword — Guide
item.description: Atsuta Jingu is one of the most venerable shrines in all of Shinto, said to have guarded the Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi — the sacred sword of the imperial regalia — for some 1,900 years, and ranking second only to Ise among the nation’s shrines. Its halls stand hushed within a deep evergreen forest of ancient camphor trees that shuts out the surrounding city, and every June the Atsuta Festival (Shobukan) fills the grounds with martial-arts dedications, hundreds of glowing makiwara lantern stands and evening fireworks, the shrine’s most spirited day of the year.

item.title: Kashima Jingu: An Ancient Shrine of Martial Arts & Deer — Guide
item.description: Kashima Jingu, with a history said to stretch back over 2,600 years, is one of Japan’s oldest and most revered shrines, historically associated with the deity of martial arts and long considered the spiritual birthplace of Japanese swordsmanship, with several historic dojos in the surrounding area still tracing their lineage to the shrine. Beyond the vermillion main gate, a dense sacred forest path leads past a small deer park (deer being messengers of the shrine’s deity) to an inner shrine and a mysterious ‘rock that binds earthquakes,’ with the shrine’s grand autumn festival drawing large crowds each September.

item.title: Musashi Ichinomiya Hikawa Shrine: A Grand Torii Avenue — Guide
item.description: Musashi Ichinomiya Hikawa Shrine holds the highest rank among the shrines of the old Musashi province, a region covering much of modern Tokyo and Saitama, with a history said to stretch back over 2,000 years. A remarkably long approach avenue, roughly 2 km and lined with towering stone and wooden torii gates, leads through a forested park to the vermillion main hall. The shrine’s grand festival each August draws large crowds with traditional rituals, food stalls and a distinctly local, community atmosphere.
